how-much-does-a-failed-print-cost-you.ht.text:
← 3D print price calculator

How much does a failed print actually cost you?

A spaghetti print at hour six of an eight-hour job still burned filament, electricity, and printer hours before it was scrapped. The failed part itself is thrown away and forgotten -- but its cost is not. It moves onto the price of the print that actually sells, because on average it takes more than one attempt to land one sellable part.

Below is the same print, priced twice, with nothing changed except the failure rate: 45g of filament at $22/kg, a 3-hour print on a $250 printer amortized over 3000 hours, 10 minutes of post-processing at $20/hr, $0.75 packaging, an 8.5% marketplace fee, and a 35% target margin.

Failure rate5%25%
Attempts needed per sellable part1.051.33
Failure buffer added to the part's cost$0.07$0.43
Total cost per sellable part$5.45$5.81
Break-even price$5.96$6.35
Suggested price (35% margin after fee)$9.64$10.29

Same filament weight, same print time, same printer, same labor and packaging -- the only input that moved is the failure rate, and it alone is worth $0.64 on the price you would need to charge to hold the same margin. That $0.64 is invisible in a per-print filament receipt, because the receipt is for the print that sold, not for the one that got scrapped an hour earlier.

Where the failure rate actually lives

It is applied only to the costs that a failed attempt still spends before it is scrapped: material, electricity, and the printer's own amortized wear. Post-processing time and packaging are not inflated by the failure rate, because a failed attempt is scrapped before it ever reaches the finishing bench -- only the successful part gets sanded, assembled, and boxed.

Common questions

How much does a failed print actually cost you?

Not the cost of the failed print itself -- that filament and time is already gone the moment the part is scrapped. What it costs you is a buffer added to the price of the print that succeeds, because on average it takes more than one attempt to land one sellable part. On an otherwise identical print, moving the failure rate from 5% to 25% raises that buffer from about $0.07 to about $0.43 per successful part, and raises the price you would need to charge (to hold the same margin) by about $0.64.

Why does a failure rate change the price of the print that succeeds?

Because a failed attempt still spent filament, electricity, and printer wear before it was scrapped, and that spend has to be recovered from somewhere -- there is no failed-print customer to bill it to. If 1 in 4 attempts fails, landing one sellable part takes on average 1 / (1 - 0.25) = 1.33 attempts, so the material, electricity, and machine-wear cost of a single attempt gets multiplied by 1.33 before it is charged to the part that actually sells. Post-processing time and packaging are not inflated the same way, because those only ever touch the part that succeeded.

Does a higher failure rate cost you money even if nothing else about the print changes?

Yes, and it is easy to miss because the failed part itself is thrown away and forgotten, while its cost quietly moves onto the next attempt's price. Two prints that are identical in every other input -- same filament weight, same print time, same printer, same labor and packaging -- price differently once their failure rates differ, because the failure-rate multiplier is applied to material, electricity, and depreciation before anything else is added.

How much would cutting your failure rate from 25% to 5% save you?

On the worked example on this page (45g filament at $22/kg, a 3-hour print, a $250 printer amortized over 3000 hours), the failure buffer alone drops from about $0.43 to about $0.07 per successful part -- roughly $0.36 saved on every part you sell, before even touching labor or packaging. Across a run of 50 parts a month that is about $18, entirely from bed adhesion, supports, and calibration rather than from filament or fees.

Price your own print

FOR MAKERS SELLING 3D-PRINTED PARTS ON ETSY, SHOPIFY, OR AT A CRAFT TABLE

"3x the filament cost" isn't a price. It's a guess.

Filament is rarely the biggest cost in a print — electricity, printer wear, failed attempts, post-processing time, and the marketplace's own cut out of your listed price all add up quietly. This free calculator prices one print from all of them, solves for what to charge so the fee and your target margin both clear, and lets you check a price you're already charging against the real break-even.

Already have a cost figure from your slicer? Here's what it does and doesn't cover.

Still pricing by "filament cost times three"? Here's what that rule can't see.

Wondering what a scrapped print actually costs you? Worked example: 5% vs. 25% failure rate.

We count only anonymous local feature events (price-calculated, price-checked, gcode_imported) so we can tell whether the calculator gets used — no costs or prices are recorded, and Do Not Track / Global Privacy Control turn it off automatically.

The Save button writes your scenario to this browser's own local storage on this device only, and Forget deletes it. Copy shareable link puts the same numbers in the page's URL fragment instead of a server — nothing about your scenario leaves your device either way, but whoever holds the link can read it.

Common questions

Why does the calculator inflate cost for a failure rate instead of just adding a flat buffer?

Because a failed print still burns filament, electricity, and printer hours before it gets scrapped, and the eventual successful print has to earn that back. On average, 1/(1 − failure rate) attempts are needed to land one sellable part, so material, electricity, and machine wear are multiplied by that factor rather than by a flat percentage guess.

Why is the marketplace fee subtracted from the price instead of added to the cost?

Because the fee is a percentage of whatever you charge, not a fixed dollar amount, so it cannot be added as a cost line the way filament or electricity can. The calculator solves price×(1 − fee%) − cost = price×(margin%) for price directly, so the number you see already clears the fee at your target margin.

Does post-processing labor or packaging get inflated by the failure rate too?

No. Post-processing time and packaging only ever happen once, on the part that actually sells — a failed print never reaches sanding or a shipping box. Only filament, electricity, and printer depreciation are multiplied, since those are what a failed attempt actually spends.

Does anything I type get uploaded?

No. Every field on this page runs in your browser only. Nothing is sent to a server, there is no account, and nothing you type is saved anywhere unless you choose to save it. Usage counting only tallies anonymous feature events, and you can turn it off with the button above. The Save button writes your scenario to this browser's own local storage on this device only, and Forget deletes it. Copy shareable link puts the same numbers in the page's URL fragment instead of a server — nothing about your scenario leaves your device either way, but whoever holds the link can read it.

Taking your prints to a craft fair or maker market? The craft fair booth calculator works out what one booth has to sell to cover its fee, mileage, and your own hours — it takes the materials percentage this tool derives and turns it into a go/no-go on the show.

Decorating garments rather than printing parts? The screen printing and embroidery price calculator costs a job the same way — a one-off setup spread over the run, plus machine time and material per piece — for screens, stitches, or DTF transfers.

vs-slicer-cost-estimate.html.text:
← 3D print price calculator

This calculator vs. your slicer's cost estimate

Slice a model in PrusaSlicer, Cura, Bambu Studio, or OrcaSlicer and it tells you two things about the job: roughly how long it will take, and roughly what the filament will cost. That cost is grams of filament multiplied by the price per kilogram you configured. It is accurate, it is useful, and it is the right number to check before you start a print.

It is not a selling price, and it is not trying to be. A price has to carry everything the spool doesn't — the power drawn for those hours, the share of the printer's own replacement cost those hours used up, the attempts that failed before one came out sellable, your finishing time, the packaging, and the percentage the marketplace takes out of whatever you charge. This page prices those directly and then solves for what to charge.

QuestionWhere to answer it
How many grams and how many hours will this model take? Your slicer — it has the geometry and the toolpath, and nothing else can answer this.
What will the filament for this print cost? Your slicer's estimate. Type the same figure into this page's grams and $/kg fields.
What did the electricity and the printer's own wear cost over those hours? This calculator — it charges power at your rate and amortizes the printer across its expected lifetime hours.
What do the prints that failed cost me on the one that sells? This calculator's failure buffer — it inflates only the per-attempt costs, not the finishing you do once.
What is my true break-even on this part, before any margin? This calculator's break-even figure.
What should I list it at so the marketplace fee and my target margin both clear? This calculator's suggested price, solved so the fee comes out of the price rather than being stacked on after it.
I'm already charging a price to match a competitor's listing. Does it actually make money? This calculator's check-a-price panel, which recomputes real profit and margin against the same break-even.
Price a print now

This tool needs no account and no upload: it is a static page, the arithmetic runs in your browser, and the figures you type stay on this device. It does not read your slicer, your printer, or your shop — you bring the grams and the hours, and it prices what happens around them.

Common questions

Is my slicer's cost estimate wrong?

No — it is right about what it measures, which is material. A slicer knows how many grams of filament the sliced model consumes and what you told it a kilogram costs, so it multiplies the two. That is an accurate material cost and a genuinely useful number. It is simply not a price: nothing in that figure is trying to cover the power the printer drew for those hours, the share of the printer's own replacement cost that those hours used up, the attempts that failed before one came out sellable, the time you spent removing supports and sanding, the box and label it ships in, or the percentage the marketplace takes out of whatever you charge.

Why not just multiply the filament cost by three?

Because the multiplier that works for one print is wrong for the next one. A 45-gram part that prints in three hours and needs no finishing has a very different cost structure from a 45-gram part that prints in fourteen hours and takes half an hour of sanding — same filament, same 3x, wildly different real cost. Multipliers hide print time, and print time is what drives electricity and printer wear. This page charges those directly instead of hoping a constant absorbs them.

How does a failed print change the number?

A failure still spent filament, electricity, and machine hours before it was scrapped. If a share of attempts fail, then on average 1/(1 − failure rate) attempts are needed to land one sellable part, so this page inflates the per-attempt costs — material, electricity, machine wear — by that factor. Post-processing and packaging are not inflated, because those only ever touch the part that actually sells. A slicer estimate has no way to know any of this; it prices one successful attempt.

Why can't I just add the marketplace fee on at the end?

Because the fee is a percentage of the price you charge, not a fixed cost you can stack on top. Adding it after the fact gives a price that looks right until the marketplace takes its cut, at which point the margin is short. This page solves price × (1 − fee%) − cost = price × (margin%) for price directly, so the number it suggests already clears the fee at the margin you asked for.

Is this page affiliated with PrusaSlicer, Cura, Bambu Studio, or OrcaSlicer?

No. This site is not affiliated with, endorsed by, or sponsored by any slicer vendor. Those names are trademarks of their owners and appear here only to describe the kind of estimate this page is contrasted with.

vs-the-3x-filament-rule.html.text:
← 3D print price calculator

This calculator vs. the 3x filament rule

Multiply the filament cost by three (or two, or four, depending who taught it to you) and call that the price — it is the fastest pricing shortcut a maker has, and for a lot of small trinkets it happens to land somewhere reasonable. It is not a calculation of anything. It has no input for print time, so a 20-minute keychain and a 20-hour functional part cut from the same filament weight get the identical price, even though one used a fraction of the electricity and printer hours the other did.

This calculator charges what actually varies by print instead of hoping a constant absorbs it: the power drawn over however many hours the print takes, the share of the printer's own replacement cost those hours used up, the attempts that failed before one came out sellable, your finishing time, the packaging, and the percentage the marketplace takes out of whatever you list.

QuestionWhere to answer it
Isn't filament cost times three close enough? Only if print time barely varies across what you sell. This calculator prices the hours directly, so a fast print and a slow print off the same filament weight stop getting the same answer.
What is a multiplier not charging me for at all? This calculator's electricity and amortized printer wear lines — a flat constant has no input for either.
What do the prints that fail cost me on the one that sells? This calculator's failure buffer, which a multiplier cannot see because it never asks your failure rate.
What is my true break-even before any margin? This calculator's break-even figure — a number a multiplier does not produce at all.
I'm already charging a price I picked by eye. Is it actually profitable? This calculator's check-a-price panel, which compares that price to the real break-even instead of to another guess.
Price a print now

This tool needs no account and no upload: it is a static page, the arithmetic runs in your browser, and the figures you type stay on this device.

Common questions

What is the 3x filament rule?

A pricing shortcut common among makers selling on Etsy, Shopify, or at a craft table: take what the filament in a print cost and multiply it by three (sometimes two, sometimes four — the constant varies by who is teaching it). It is fast, needs no other numbers, and for a lot of small trinkets it happens to land somewhere reasonable. It is not a calculation of anything; it is a habit that has not yet been tested against a print that breaks it.

Why does the same multiplier work for one print and fail for another?

Because filament weight and print time are not the same thing, and only one of them drives most of the real cost. A 20-gram print that takes 20 minutes and a 20-gram print that takes 8 hours can cost the same in filament and wildly different amounts in electricity and printer wear — the multiplier gives them the same price either way. The rule is really a bet that time-per-gram stays roughly constant across everything you print. Miniatures and multi-hour functional parts do not share that ratio, so one flat constant cannot price both correctly.

What does a flat multiplier leave out completely?

Three things it has no input for at all: the printer itself wearing out over its service life, the prints that fail partway through and still burn filament and hours before they are scrapped, and the percentage a marketplace takes out of whatever price you list — which is a cut of the price, not a cost you can multiply into it. A multiplier is silent on all three because it was never given the print time, the failure rate, or the fee percentage to begin with.

Can a multiplier tell me if I am pricing below break-even?

No — it has no break-even to compare against, because it never separately totals electricity, amortized printer wear, and the failure buffer. This calculator does, and the check-a-price panel takes a price you are already charging (to match a competitor's listing, say) and shows the real profit and margin against that break-even, rather than against a guess.

Is a flat multiplier ever fine to use?

For a quick mental check on a small, fast, low-stakes print, sure — it costs nothing to eyeball. The risk is treating it as a price for everything, especially long or power-hungry prints, where the gap between the guess and the real cost is largest and least visible until a run of orders quietly loses money.
